questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An account that would swallow any outcome
questions.learningObjective: Identify an unfalsifiable explanation in a field note
questions.stem: A biologist explains every nest failure by invoking an unseen predator. What is the flaw?

options.text: The account explains any outcome, so it predicts none

questions.explanation: An account that fits every possible result cannot be tested against new evidence. The tempting idea that covering all cases makes it strong actually makes it empty.
questions.hint: Ask what would disprove the account.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Eliminating an account on scope rather than preference
questions.learningObjective: Judge elimination by scope not taste
questions.stem: A field team rejects an account because it is less elegant, not because it fails. What error?

options.text: It proves the account is false
It eliminates by preference rather than by scope or evidence

questions.explanation: Elimination should rest on evidence or scope, not on taste. The tempting idea that elegance decides between accounts confuses preference with proof.
questions.hint: Require evidence, not taste.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A source that does not yet exist in the record
questions.learningObjective: Flag a source not yet in the record
questions.stem: A report cites a survey that has not been conducted yet. What is the flaw?

options.text: It assumes the survey will agree
It relies on a source that does not yet exist in the record

questions.explanation: A planned source is not evidence until it exists and is examined. The tempting idea that a future survey supports a present claim is premature.
questions.hint: Wait for the source to exist.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A prediction confirmed after it was named
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a post-hoc prediction counts as support

stimulus.body: In a field biologist's survey, a researcher names a predicted species count after seeing the data, then claims the survey confirmed the prediction. The client asks whether this counts as support.

questions.stem: Does this count as genuine support?

options.text: Yes, because the researcher is expert
No, because the sample is small
options.misconception: raises a size issue not the flaw

options.text: No, because the prediction followed the data

questions.explanation: A prediction must precede the data to test an account. Naming it afterward fits the story to the result. The tempting idea that a match is confirmation ignores timing.
questions.hint: Check when the prediction was made.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Eliminating an account by assuming away the evidence
questions.stem: A team rules out an account by assuming its key evidence is unreliable. What flaw?

options.text: It proves the account is false
It eliminates the account by assuming away its evidence

questions.explanation: Dismissing evidence by assumption removes the account's support without testing it. The elimination is circular. The tempting idea that doubt equals disproof is unsound.
questions.hint: Test the evidence, do not assume it away.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A statement with a second account attached to it
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a hedged claim carrying a backup explanation
questions.stem: A field note says a nest failed, adding 'unless a storm caused it.' What is the problem?

options.text: The hedge supplies a second account that swallows the first

questions.explanation: A hedge that supplies an alternative for every case makes the original claim unfalsifiable. The tempting idea that covering contingencies is careful actually weakens the claim.
questions.hint: Check whether the hedge can be tested.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A compromise between two accounts
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a compromise account is coherent
questions.stem: Two biologists propose a hybrid account blending their rival explanations. Is the hybrid automatically better?

options.text: Yes, because it includes both views
No, unless it explains more and predicts new cases

questions.explanation: A hybrid must be judged by explanatory and predictive success, not by including both views. The tempting idea that compromise yields truth is unfounded.
questions.hint: Test the hybrid against new data.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two explanations that are not rivals
questions.stem: Two accounts explain different aspects of the same event. Are they rivals?

options.text: Yes, because only one cause can operate
No, because they address different aspects and can both hold
No, because both are probably true
Yes, because they disagree on detail

questions.explanation: Explanations that address different aspects are not mutually exclusive. The tempting idea that any two accounts must compete ignores their distinct scopes.
questions.hint: Check what each account actually explains.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a new account would have to do to earn a place
questions.learningObjective: State the burden for a new explanation
questions.stem: A biologist proposes a new account of a decline. What must it show?

options.text: It must come from a senior researcher
It must be simpler than the current account
It must explain more and predict cases the current account cannot

questions.explanation: A new account earns its place by superior explanatory and predictive power. Simplicity, authority, or prior belief alone do not suffice. The tempting idea that novelty is enough is mistaken.
questions.hint: Require new predictive success.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Putting rival accounts through a trial in order
questions.stem: A team tests rival accounts one at a time in a set order. What risk arises?

options.text: It proves the first account is best
Early acceptance may stop testing of better later accounts

questions.explanation: Sequential testing risks stopping at the first adequate account. Better accounts may be missed. The tempting idea that passing a first test settles the matter is premature.
questions.hint: Keep testing after a pass.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: How a document came to be written and kept
questions.learningObjective: Assess provenance of a field record
questions.stem: A field record's value depends on who wrote it and why. What must be checked?

options.text: Its author, purpose, and chain of custody

questions.explanation: Provenance shapes reliability. Without knowing author, purpose, and custody, the record's weight is unknown. The tempting idea that an old record is automatically reliable is mistaken.
questions.hint: Establish provenance first.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A document used for a purpose it was not written for
questions.learningObjective: Detect misuse of a document's purpose
questions.stem: A permit record is used to estimate species abundance. What is the flaw?

options.text: The document was not created to measure abundance

questions.explanation: A document's original purpose limits what it can support. Using it for another purpose needs justification. The tempting idea that any record answers any question is unsound.
questions.hint: Match the question to the document's purpose.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A record read against its intended reader
questions.learningObjective: Read a record with its audience in mind
questions.stem: A field log written for managers is read as raw data. What risk?

options.text: It proves the log is false
The log may summarize or omit detail for its audience

questions.explanation: A record shaped for an audience may compress or select information. Reading it as raw data risks misinterpretation. The tempting idea that a written record is complete is mistaken.
questions.hint: Consider the intended reader.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What the absence of a record can be asked to show
questions.learningObjective: Limit what missing records can prove
questions.stem: A species is declared absent because no record exists. What is the flaw?

options.text: Absence of a record is not evidence of absence

questions.explanation: Missing records may reflect limited search or preservation, not absence. The tempting idea that no record means no species overstates the evidence.
questions.hint: Ask how thoroughly the area was searched.

questions.hint: Establish provenance first.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A document used for a purpose it was not written for
questions.stem: A permit record is used to estimate species abundance. What is the flaw?

options.text: The document was not created to measure abundance

questions.explanation: A document's original purpose limits what it can support. Using it for another purpose needs justification. The tempting idea that any record answers any question is unsound.
questions.hint: Match the question to the document's purpose.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A record read against its intended reader
questions.learningObjective: Read a record with its audience in mind
questions.stem: A field log written for managers is read as raw data. What risk?

options.text: It proves the log is false
The log may summarize or omit detail for its audience

questions.explanation: A record shaped for an audience may compress or select information. Reading it as raw data risks misinterpretation. The tempting idea that a written record is complete is mistaken.
questions.hint: Consider the intended reader.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What the absence of a record can be asked to show
questions.learningObjective: Limit what missing records can prove
questions.stem: A species is declared absent because no record exists. What is the flaw?

options.text: Absence of a record is not evidence of absence

questions.explanation: Missing records may reflect limited search or preservation, not absence. The tempting idea that no record means no species overstates the evidence.
questions.hint: Ask how thoroughly the area was searched.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A category applied to a period before it existed
questions.stem: A biologist labels a 19th-century specimen with a modern category. What is the flaw?

options.text: The category did not exist in that period

questions.explanation: Applying a category before it existed distorts the historical record. The tempting idea that modern terms clarify old data risks anachronism.
questions.hint: Check when the category was defined.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a document of one kind can be used to show
questions.learningObjective: Limit claims to a document's type
questions.stem: A sketch map is used to prove population density. What is the flaw?

options.text: A sketch map cannot support a population claim

questions.explanation: A document's type limits what it can show. A sketch map shows location, not population. The tempting idea that any document supports any claim is unsound.
questions.hint: Match claim to document type.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The place and date a document claims for itself
questions.stem: A document's stated date and place are taken at face value. What should be checked?

options.text: Whether the date and place are internally and externally consistent

questions.explanation: A document's self-claimed origin must be corroborated. Internal consistency and external evidence both matter. The tempting idea that a stated date is true is naive.
questions.hint: Corroborate the origin claim.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A copy standing in for the thing it copies
questions.learningObjective: Assess what a copy can show
questions.stem: A photocopy of a field note is treated as the original. What is lost?

options.text: It proves the copy is false
Material features and possible alterations are hidden

questions.explanation: A copy may conceal material features, annotations, or alterations present in the original. The tempting idea that a clear copy equals the original is mistaken.
questions.hint: Check the original when possible.

provenance.author: bank-team-seminar
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a copy of a summary can be asked to support
questions.learningObjective: Limit claims from a copied summary
questions.stem: A copy of a summary is used to prove original detail. What is the flaw?

options.text: A summary copy cannot support claims about original detail

questions.explanation: A summary by definition omits detail. A copy of it cannot restore what was omitted. The tempting idea that a summary preserves all detail is false.
questions.hint: Go to the original for detail.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What survives, and what the surviving record is evidence of
questions.stem: A species list survives from one survey and is treated as typical. What is the flaw?

options.text: Survival does not show the record is representative

questions.explanation: What survives may be unrepresentative due to selection or chance. The tempting idea that surviving records depict typical conditions is unsupported.
questions.hint: Ask how the record was selected.
